title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
prompt:
Two classes each keep a linked list of quiz scores, already sorted ascending. Merge them into one sorted list by splicing together the existing nodes, and return its head.

Write mergeTwoLists(list1, list2). The helpers ListNode, fromArray and toArray are at the top; keep them.

  • toArray(mergeTwoLists(fromArray([1, 2, 4]), fromArray([1, 3, 4]))) gives [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]
  • mergeTwoLists(null, null) returns null
  • toArray(mergeTwoLists(null, fromArray([0]))) gives [0]

Constraints: 0 to 50 nodes in each list; values from -100 to 100. Target: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space.

tests.name: one list entirely before the other
splices the original nodes

hints: Trigger: "merge two sorted ..." = two pointers, one per list, always take the smaller head. With linked lists, add the dummy head trick.
Create const dummy = new ListNode(0) and a tail pointer starting at it. Each step, attach the smaller of the two current nodes to tail.next, advance that list, advance tail. Return dummy.next.

Shape:

while (a !== null && b !== null) {
  if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }
  else { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
  tail = tail.next;
}
tail.next = a !== null ? a : b;
return dummy.next;
explain:
Time O(n + m): every node is attached exactly once. Space O(1) extra: you relink existing nodes, you don't copy. The dummy node removes the "is the result still empty?" special case; it is the most useful linked-list trick there is.

Say it: "Two pointers, one per list, plus a dummy head. Take the smaller node each step, then attach the leftover tail. O(n + m) time, O(1) space." This is also the merge step of merge sort, and the building block for merging k sorted lists with a heap.
